title: The Atlas concedes that permanent bans are practically unenforceable and asks moderators to judge recidivism
content:
A.2.7.1.2.1.1.4, titled Intrinsic Limitations, states the position plainly: "Given the digital nature of these communication channels and the consequent practical unenforceability of permanent bannings, responsible moderators are expected to have to deal with recurring banned users under new aliases. Responsible moderators must exercise best judgement when suspecting a user to be a banned user under a different guise and when assessing whether they pose a risk of recidivism."

A rule set writing down that its own sanction cannot be enforced is unusual, and the honesty is the useful part. Pseudonymous accounts are free to create, so a ban removes an identity rather than a person. Pretending otherwise would leave moderators either enforcing a fiction or improvising outside policy.

What the provision does instead is convert the rule from a guarantee into a *cost*: a banned user can return, but must abandon their reputation and standing, and faces re-exclusion on suspicion. That is a meaningful deterrent even though it is not a barrier.

It also legitimises action on suspicion, which matters because identity cannot be proven either way. A moderator may act on a judgment that an account is a returning banned user without having to demonstrate it — and the standard offered is "risk of recidivism," which is forward-looking behaviour rather than backward-looking identification.

The cost is a discretionary power with no evidentiary standard, sitting beside an unbanning process (A.2.7.1.2.1.1.3) whose ecosystem-wide reinstatement applies only "where identity can be proven." Exclusion may act on suspicion; readmission requires proof. That asymmetry is defensible for a small governance forum, and it is worth naming as one.
description: Given the digital nature of the channels, moderators are expected to face banned users returning under new aliases and must use best judgment when they suspect it.
